planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; needs steadier moisture than its blue-flowered Sisyrinchium relatives.

directions: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, since golden-eyed grass is native to coastal marshes, seeps, and wet meadows from California to British Columbia and needs steady moisture to thrive, unlike its blue-flowered relatives. Bright yellow, six-petaled flowers streaked with maroon veining open in succession atop flattened, iris-like foliage from spring into summer, drawing small native bees and syrphid flies. It naturalizes readily by self-seeding in boggy or streamside plantings and rain gardens, forming expanding clumps over a few seasons. Site it in a low spot or near a pond edge where it won't dry out during summer.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seed experiences natural winter chilling, into deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this taprooted native transplants poorly once established, so sow it in its permanent site. Requires 60–90 days cold-moist stratification and germination is slow and uneven even after chilling.

directions: Direct sow in fall so seed experiences natural winter chilling, into deep, well-drained soil in full sun, since arrowleaf balsamroot forms a long, woody taproot and transplants poorly once established. It is one of the great signature wildflowers of the Rocky Mountain and Intermountain West foothills, carpeting sagebrush steppe and open slopes with large, sunflower-like yellow blooms above silvery, arrow-shaped leaves each spring. The flowers are a major early-season nectar source for native bees, and the foliage and seed heads are important forage for elk, deer, and small mammals across its range. Once established, plants are extremely long-lived and drought tolerant, requiring no irrigation, but they resent disturbance and often do not bloom until their second or third year, so plant them where they can be left undisturbed.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall into rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, matching the limestone canyons and rocky slopes of the Southwest and southern Rockies where cliff fendlerbush grows wild.

directions: Plant container stock in fall into rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, matching the limestone canyons and rocky slopes of the Southwest and southern Rockies where cliff fendlerbush grows wild. In late spring it produces an abundant flush of four-petaled, white to pale-pink, sweetly fragrant flowers resembling mock orange blossoms, drawing native bees, hawk moths, and hummingbirds to an otherwise sparse rocky landscape. It is highly drought- and cold-tolerant once established and needs no supplemental irrigation, making it well suited to xeriscape and native rock-garden plantings. Deer tend to browse it lightly, and its dense, twiggy branching provides good cover for small birds.

planting.note: Scarify seed lightly and direct sow in fall with the first autumn rains, into well-drained soil in full sun, allowing arroyo lupine to germinate and grow through the mild California winter as it does in the wild.

directions: Scarify seed lightly and direct sow in fall with the first autumn rains, into well-drained soil in full sun, allowing arroyo lupine to germinate and grow through the mild California winter as it does in the wild. Thick spikes of deep blue-purple, pea-like flowers with white banners bloom heavily in spring, making this one of the showiest and most reliable of the California annual lupines for mass wildflower plantings and roadside meadows. Like other lupines, its roots fix nitrogen and improve soil, and the flowers are an important early-season nectar and pollen source for native bees and butterflies, including several skipper species that use lupines as larval hosts. Plants self-seed readily in disturbed, sunny sites, so a single fall sowing can produce recurring displays in following years.
